39: The Beijing Daxing International Airport, 46 kilometres south of Tiananmen Square, opened on 30 September 2019. Construction of this mega-project began in 2014, and at its peak there were more than 40,000 workers on site. The terminal is compactly designed so that the maximum number of aircraft can park directly at the positions closest to the centre of the terminal, which brings great convenience to passengers. The terminal has 82 boarding gates, yet after passing the security check passengers need less than eight minutes to reach any one of them. The airport is designed to handle 300 take-offs and landings an hour. Its annual passenger volume will reach 100 million by 2040, and it is expected to become the busiest airport in the world.
40: Journey to the West is perhaps the most influential of the four great classic novels of Chinese literature and, of course, the one best known abroad. The novel depicts the arduous journey of the famous monk Xuanzang, accompanied by three disciples, across western China to India in search of Buddhist scriptures. Although the theme of the story is based on Buddhism, the novel draws heavily on Chinese folk tales and myths and creates a variety of vivid human and animal characters. The best known is Sun Wukong, whose battles against all kinds of demons and monsters are familiar to almost every Chinese child.
41:
Dream of the Red Chamber is a novel written by Cao Xueqin in the 18th century. Drawing on his own bitter personal experience, Cao tells the tragic love story between Jia Baoyu and Lin Daiyu. The book contains about 30 major characters and more than 400 minor ones, each portrayed so vividly that they have a distinct personality. The novel describes in detail the rise and fall of four aristocratic families and reflects the hidden crises and intricate social conflicts of feudal society.

Dream of the Red Chamber combines realism and romanticism and has strong artistic appeal. It is generally regarded as the greatest Chinese novel and one of the greatest literary creations in the world.
42: Water Margin is one of the four great classic novels of Chinese literature. Based on the story of the historical figure Song Jiang and his companions rebelling against the feudal emperor, the novel has been loved by Chinese readers for centuries. It is no exaggeration to say that almost every Chinese is familiar with some of its main characters. The novel's exciting stories have been retold again and again in teahouses, on the stage, on radio and television, on cinema screens and in countless homes. In fact, the novel's influence has long reached beyond national borders. More and more foreign readers also find its stories vivid, moving and full of interest.
43: The Romance of the Three Kingdoms is a famous Chinese historical novel written in the 14th century. Set against the history of the Three Kingdoms period, this literary work describes the wars among the kingdoms of Wei, Shu and Wu from the second half of the 2nd century AD to the second half of the 3rd century AD. The novel portrays nearly a thousand characters and countless historical events. Although most of these characters and events are based on real history, they have all been romanticized and dramatized to varying degrees. The Romance of the Three Kingdoms is a recognized literary masterpiece. Since its publication the novel has continued to attract generation after generation of readers and has had a broad and lasting influence on Chinese culture.
44: With its brilliant colours and elegant appearance, the peony symbolizes peace and prosperity and is therefore called the "king of flowers" in China. Peonies are cultivated and planted in many parts of the country. Over the centuries many poems and paintings have been created in praise of the peony. In the Tang Dynasty peonies were widely planted in imperial gardens and were acclaimed as the national flower, and so they became especially popular. In the 10th century the ancient city of Luoyang became the centre of peony cultivation, and it has kept that position to this day. Now thousands of domestic tourists flock to Luoyang for the annual peony festival, admiring the unique beauty of Luoyang peonies and at the same time exploring the history of this ancient capital of nine dynasties.
45: The plum blossom ranks first among China's ten most famous flowers. It originated in southern China and has a history of more than 3,000 years of cultivation and planting. In the depths of winter, plum blossoms of every colour bloom proudly in the wind and snow, undaunted by the cold. In traditional Chinese culture the plum blossom symbolizes strength, purity and elegance, and inspires people to press on despite hardships. Since ancient times many poets and painters have drawn inspiration from plum blossoms and created countless enduring works. Ordinary people love them too, and often use them to decorate their homes during Spring Festival. Nanjing has made the plum blossom its city flower and holds a plum blossom festival every year, when thousands of people brave the cold to admire the blossoms in the snow on Plum Blossom Hill.
46: The lotus flower is one of China's famous flowers and is deeply loved by the people. The lakes and ponds in many parts of China are suitable for growing lotus. Lotus flowers are brightly coloured, opening in the early morning in summer and closing at night. The flowering period lasts two to three months, attracting visitors from all over to admire them. The lotus has many functions: it can green the water surface, beautify gardens, purify water, reduce pollution and improve the environment. Facing the blazing sun without fear and rising from the mud unstained, the lotus symbolizes purity and elegance and is often used as a metaphor for noble character; it has always been an important subject for poets and painters. Places where lotuses bloom are also frequented by many photography enthusiasts.
47: Chinese idioms are a unique form of expression in the Chinese language, most of them made up of four Chinese characters. They are highly concise and fixed in form, yet they usually express profound meanings in a vivid way. Most Chinese idioms come from ancient Chinese literature and are often related to certain myths, legends or historical events. Without knowing the origin of an idiom, it is hard to understand its exact meaning. Learning Chinese idioms therefore helps people better understand traditional Chinese culture. Idioms are widely used in everyday conversation and in literary creation. Using them appropriately can make one's language more expressive and one's communication more effective.
48: China has a vast territory and a large population, and in many places people speak their own local dialects. Dialects differ greatly in pronunciation but relatively little in vocabulary and grammar. Some dialects, especially those of the north and the south, differ so much that speakers of different dialects often find it hard to understand each other. Dialects are regarded as an integral part of local culture, but in recent years the number of people who can speak them has kept declining. To encourage people to speak their local languages more, some local governments have taken measures such as offering dialect classes in schools and broadcasting dialect programmes on radio and television, in the hope of preserving local cultural heritage.
49: Chinese is now the language with the largest number of native speakers in the world. An important difference between Chinese and Western languages is that it is made up of square characters rather than letters. Among the writing systems still in use, Chinese is the oldest. In China people from different regions may not understand each other's dialects, but because Chinese characters have a unified written form, they have almost no difficulty communicating. Chinese has played an important role in uniting the Chinese nation throughout history. Today, with China's rapid economic growth and growing global influence, more and more people in other countries are beginning to learn Chinese.
50: In recent years more and more museums in China have opened to the public free of charge. Both the number of exhibitions and the number of visitors have grown markedly. Long queues in front of some popular museums have become a common sight, and these museums have had to take measures to limit visitor numbers. Today exhibitions take an ever greater variety of forms. Some large museums use advanced technologies such as multimedia and virtual reality to make their exhibitions more attractive. Many museums also hold online exhibitions, where people can view rare exhibits on the internet. However, for most visitors, seeing the exhibits in person is still more appealing.
51: China is paying more and more attention to public libraries and encouraging people to make full use of them. Recently published statistics show that the number of public libraries in China is growing year by year. Through renovation and expansion, many libraries have created quieter and more comfortable environments for readers. Large public libraries not only provide a wide range of reference materials but also hold lectures, exhibitions and other activities on a regular basis. In recent years many digital libraries have appeared, which has saved the space needed to store books. Some libraries have also introduced self-service systems, making it easier for readers to borrow and return books and further meeting their needs.
52: In recent years the Chinese government has further increased investment in building gymnasiums and stadiums to better meet people's rapidly growing demand for fitness. Besides building new ones, many cities have also taken measures such as converting old factories and commercial buildings to increase the number of local sports venues. With government funding, more and more venues are open to the public free of charge or for only a small fee. Many of them have greatly improved their service quality by applying modern information technology. People can conveniently book venues and pay online. It is foreseeable that, as sports facilities keep improving, more and more people will go to gymnasiums and stadiums to exercise.
53: In the past, owning a private car was a luxury for most Chinese people. Today private cars can be seen everywhere in China. Cars have become an indispensable part of people's lives: they not only drive to and from work but also often go on trips by car. In some cities the number of cars has grown so fast that traffic congestion and the shortage of parking spaces have become increasingly serious, and the municipal governments have had to issue new rules limiting the number of cars on the road. As air pollution worsens, more and more people now choose to buy new energy vehicles, and the Chinese government has also taken measures to support their development.
54: China now has the largest and fastest high-speed rail network in the world. The speed of high-speed trains will continue to rise, and more cities will build high-speed rail stations. High-speed rail has greatly shortened people's travel time. Compared with flying, the outstanding advantage of high-speed trains is punctuality, since they are basically unaffected by weather or traffic control. High-speed rail has greatly changed the way Chinese people live. Today it has become the first choice of transport for many people on business trips. More and more people also travel by high-speed rail during holidays. Many young people even choose to work in one city and live in a neighbouring one, commuting by high-speed train every day.
55: Bicycles were once the main means of transport in both urban and rural China, and the country was once called the "kingdom of bicycles". Today, as urban traffic congestion and air pollution worsen, cycling has become popular again. Recently Chinese entrepreneurs combined mobile internet technology with the traditional bicycle and invented a business model known as shared bikes. The arrival of shared bikes has made cycling more convenient: with just a mobile phone people can use a shared bike at any time. To encourage people to cycle, many cities have built cycle lanes. Now more and more Chinese also like to keep fit by cycling.
56: Taihu Lake is a freshwater lake in eastern China. Covering an area of 2,250 square kilometres, it is the third largest freshwater lake in China, after Poyang and Dongting. Taihu has about 90 islands, ranging in size from a few square metres to several square kilometres. It is famous for its unique "Taihu stones", which are often used to decorate traditional Chinese gardens. The lake is also known for its highly productive fishery. Since the late 1970s, fishing for fish and crabs has been extremely important to the residents along the lake and has contributed significantly to the economy of the surrounding area. The Taihu region is one of China's ceramics bases, and the ceramics factories of Yixing there produce the world-famous Yixing clay teapots.
57: Qinghai Lake lies at an elevation of 3,205 metres, about 100 kilometres west of Xining, the capital of Qinghai Province. It is the largest saltwater lake in China, with an area of 4,317 square kilometres and a maximum depth of 25.5 metres. Twenty-three rivers flow into the lake, most of them seasonal. Eighty percent of the lake's water comes from five major rivers. Qinghai Lake sits at the crossroads of several bird migration routes across Asia, and many birds use it as a stopover on their migrations. On the western side of the lake is the famous "Bird Island", which attracts birdwatchers from all over the world. Every summer tourists also come here to watch international cycling races.
